Nigeria’s external reserves declined by $369m in four days, even as the naira appreciated by N19 against the dollar at the official foreign exchange market, highlighting continued pressure on the country’s foreign currency buffers. Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria showed that reserves fell from $54.358bn on Monday to $53.989bn on Thursday, reflecting persistent demand for foreign exchange and pressure on the CBN’s ability to build its external buffers. The naira’s appreciation on Thursday followed the CBN’s approval of increased dollar cash sales to Bureau De Change operators, a measure aimed at improving dollar availability in the retail foreign exchange market. The local currency appreciated to N1,378/$ on Thursday from N1,397/$ recorded on Wednesday at the official market, reversing part of the losses suffered in recent weeks. However, the recovery comes after the naira shed N43.5 against the dollar between 13 November and 25 November, reflecting renewed pressure on the FX market. The reserves decline also extends a recent downward trend. Between 6 November, when reserves stood at $55.060bn, and 27 November, they fell by $1.071bn, reflecting growing pressure on Nigeria’s external liquidity position. The reserves drawdown has coincided with increased demand for dollars ahead of the festive season, election-related spending and foreign portfolio investors adjusting their positions towards the end of the year. High energy costs, inefficient ports hurting Nigerian exports – NEXIM Bank Naira gains N19 amid fresh CBN forex intervention Cardoso urges banks to bridge exporters’ financing gaps CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso, had identified seasonal demand from businesses seeking to hedge against exchange rate movements, portfolio investors repositioning their investments and increased spending associated with the 2027 general elections as factors contributing to pressure on the FX market. The CBN has also been supplying dollars to the FX market to moderate volatility and meet demand. Such interventions can draw down external reserves when dollar sales exceed fresh foreign currency inflows. Cardoso, however, described the recent reserve decline as temporary, maintaining that Nigeria’s external buffers remained adequate to meet its obligations. He also pointed to strong diaspora remittances and a favourable current account position as sources of support for the country’s external position. Speaking on Tuesday after the 308th meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee, CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso, said on naira and reserves volatility: “These are all seasonal. And we believe very strongly that as we go into the next year, we will find a major moderation in the volatility that you have seen.” Thursday’s naira appreciation followed the CBN’s decision to expand dollar cash allocations to BDC operators. Under the revised arrangement, banks can sell up to $1m in physical cash to eligible BDCs, compared with the previous limit of $150,000 weekly, of which only 25 per cent could be accessed in cash. Experts say the policy is expected to improve dollar availability in the retail market and ease pressure on the parallel market, although its impact on overall foreign exchange liquidity remains to be seen. Odinaka Anudu
